Acrobot.name: acrobot
Acrobot.doc:
Acrobot-v1. Render state ``[theta1, theta2]`` — 2 of the observation's 6 dims.

Two traps in the source, both silent. ``xys = np.array([[0,0], p1, p2])[:, ::-1]`` **swaps x and
y**, so link 2 hangs off ``(p1_y, p1_x)``; and ``p2`` is computed but never drawn, because only two
``thetas`` are zipped against three points. The ground rule is ``pygame.draw.line``, which
TRUNCATES its float y (363.6364 -> row 363) — rounding puts the whole line one row off, 1000 px a
frame, which looks like a rasterizer bug rather than a coordinate one.

``step`` takes 3 discrete actions — torque -1, 0, +1 — as one floored float. Dynamical state
``[theta1, theta2, dtheta1, dtheta2]``, one RK4 step at ``dt = 0.2``; tracks the reference to
**4.4e-13 over 100 steps, 1.1e-16 after one**. The widest spread in the family and the fewest
bit-identical steps (15.4%), which is what a chaotic double pendulum is supposed to do to two
trajectories that started one ulp apart.

CartPole.name: cartpole
CartPole.doc:
CartPole-v1. Render state ``[x, theta]`` — 2 of the observation's 4 dims.

Draw order, from the source: cart quad, pole quad, axle disc, then ``hline`` for the track, which
is painted LAST and therefore over the cart. The cart is axis-aligned, so its ``aapolygon`` takes
SDL_gfx's solid ``hline``/``vline`` short-circuit and is not anti-aliased at all; only the pole is.

``step`` takes 2 discrete actions — 0 push left, 1 push right — as one float per environment,
floored. Dynamical state ``[x, x_dot, theta, theta_dot]``, Euler at ``tau = 0.02``; tracks the
reference to **4.4e-14 over 100 steps, 1.1e-16 after one**.

DMCCheetahRun.name: dmc-cheetah-run

visual_fidelity.measured_at: 84 px, 64 states per domain from sample_states (the domain's own initialize_episode plus a 0-40 step random-action rollout), default appearance, H200 / driver 590.48.01 / MUJOCO_GL=egl, mujoco 3.11.0 + mujoco-warp 3.11.0, against dm_control's physics.render at camera 0

DMCCheetahRun.visual_note: The frame is MJWarp's raytrace of the same scene, not dm_control's own raster. Two named mechanisms carry the residual, both measured per surface off MuJoCo's segmentation buffer: (1) the skybox is an 800x4800 gradient with mark="random" specks and MJWarp samples it with one unfiltered tap, which is 48-89% of the frame on cheetah/hopper/walker at mean 4.1-4.7/255 and is what holds SSIM down; (2) the checker floor is MINIFIED and MJWarp has no level-of-detail selection, so where MuJoCo's mipmap shows one grey (far-band luminance spread 0.1 on humanoid) MJWarp paints full contrast (9.7). Suitable for generating training data live -- the frame is a function of the state and the appearance knobs are per-environment tensors. NOT a substitute for a stored dataset when a policy will be evaluated on official dm_control pixels: the train and eval pixel distributions differ by the amount above and nothing here measures what that costs a policy. Closing it needs plane-texture level-of-detail in mujoco_warp's render kernel, which needs ray differentials it does not compute.
DMCCheetahRun.doc:
DM Control cheetah-run at camera 0, a mode="trackcom" camera.

VISUAL TIER -- these are NOT the official pixels. The frame is MJWarp's raytrace of dm_control's own scene at dm_control's own camera, which lands on MuJoCo's cam_xpos to 1e-8 m; measured against physics.render it is mean 5.01/255 with 88.2% of pixels within 8/255 and SSIM 0.661. The residual is the unfiltered speckled skybox and the minified checker floor. Good for generating training data live; not interchangeable with a stored dataset of official pixels. See visual_note.

FetchPickAndPlace.name: fetch-pickandplace
FetchPickAndPlace.parity_note: TWO declared residuals, measured separately, both structural to the backend rather than to this scene. (1) THE ROBOT'S 18 MESHES ARE SHADED PER PIXEL AND MuJoCo SHADES THEM PER VERTEX. MuJoCo draws meshes as triangles with Gouraud interpolation of vertex colours; an analytic per-pixel Blinn-Phong evaluation lands within a level or two of it and not on it. The robot is 8.9% of the frame and carries essentially all of the interior residual -- 0.8% of interior pixels, at an interior mean of 0.009/255, i.e. the disagreement is one level where it exists at all. This is the same limit the OGBench port records and refuted three ways (Gouraud over MuJoCo's own tessellation scored WORSE than plain per-pixel there), and it bites here because a Fetch mover is 9% of the frame rather than 20 pixels. (2) THE TRANSLUCENT MOCAP MARKERS ARE NOT DRAWN. robot0:mocap carries a 1 cm cube at alpha 0.7 and three 2 m crosshair bars at alpha 0.1; mujoco_warp's shader reads only color[0..2] and packs a constant 255, so it has no alpha path at all and would paint them opaque saturated green. Measured against a reference with them hidden: they are 1.2-1.5% of ALL pixels (mean 0.32/255) and 0.000002 of INTERIOR pixels -- a translucent bar over a flat surface leaves no flat 3x3 neighbourhood, so none of it reaches the interior metric. That is also why mocap is not in the state: it reaches no other pixel. What is NOT in these numbers, because it was found and fixed: the float->uint8 quantisation rule (mujoco_warp truncates, GL rounds), worth interior 0.791 -> 0.9988 on its own. The static 91% of the frame -- floor, table, skybox -- is exact by construction, because it is baked through MuJoCo itself.

State is qpos plus the 3-D goal; the sparse variant differs from its siblings in the reward and the observation container, neither of which reaches the renderer, so it shares the PickAndPlace plate and model.

DMCHopperHop.visual_note: The frame is MJWarp's raytrace of the same scene, not dm_control's own raster. Suitable for generating training data live -- the frame is a function of the state and the appearance knobs are per-environment tensors. NOT a substitute for a stored dataset when a policy will be evaluated on official dm_control pixels: the train and eval pixel distributions differ by the amount above and nothing here measures what that costs a policy. MountainCarContinuous.doc:
MountainCarContinuous-v0. Nearly two envs for the price of one — but not quite.

``continuous_mountain_car.render`` is byte-identical to ``mountain_car.render`` apart from one
comment (checked by diffing the two sources), which makes it very tempting to reuse the renderer
unchanged. That is wrong by 23,984 pixels across 64 frames, because the flag is drawn from
``self.goal_position`` and the two envs do not agree on it: **0.45 here, 0.5 for MountainCar-v0**,
with a source comment attributing the difference to a third-party port. Identical draw code over a
different constant is exactly the class of error a "looks the same" check misses and a pixel diff
catches immediately.

The same trap runs through the physics, one level deeper: ``step`` here takes one CONTINUOUS force
in [-1, 1] scaled by ``power``, and it computes in **float32** where MountainCar-v0 computes in
float64 (see ``_dynamics``). Seeded from a state the reference has already stored, agreement is
**exact — exact_frac 1.0, max deviation 0.0 over 16 x 100 steps**; seeded from a freshly reset
float64 state the reference's own first step is in a different dtype regime and the trajectory
differs by up to one float32 ulp of position (1.2e-07).

MountainCar.name: mountain-car
MountainCar.doc:
MountainCar-v0. Render state ``[position]`` — one number for a 400x600 frame.

The terrain is 99 ``pygame.draw.aalines`` segments, a sub-pixel AA path unrelated to gfxdraw's and
not reimplemented; it is also a constant of the environment rather than of the state, so it is
rasterised once by pygame and cached. That is exact by construction and free per frame. Everything
the state moves — the car quad and its two wheels — is pure gfxdraw and exact by the rules in
``render/gfxdraw``. The flag is drawn AFTER the car in the reference, so it cannot join the baked
layer; it is gfxdraw too, so it does not need to.

``step`` takes 3 discrete actions — 0 push left, 1 coast, 2 push right — as one floored float.
Dynamical state ``[position, velocity]``; tracks the reference to **3.3e-16 over 100 steps,
5.4e-20 after one**, the tightest in the family because one step is three float64 operations and a
cosine.

PointmazeLargeNavigate.name: pointmaze-large-navigate
PointmazeLargeNavigate.parity_note: AGENT-PIXEL PARITY (supersample 2, against MuJoCo at its default offsamples=4, 25 cells x 64 states). Every disagreement is inside the agent's own silhouette: the baked plate is exact by construction, non-agent pixels are 99.88-99.99% bit-identical, and that residual is the reference's multisampling bleeding agent colour into neighbouring wall/floor pixels. On agent-interior pixels (eroded by one, so coverage is not in play) the shader reaches 48-84% within 1/255 for pointmaze (mean 1.2-2.5/255), 0-51% for antmaze and 0-3% for humanoidmaze. The legged numbers are not a shading result: at the official whole-maze camera the ant is 12-70 px and the humanoid 4-21 px of 50176, and eroding leaves as few as 1 interior pixel, so their agreement is a statement about a silhouette under the reference's coverage rule. Against a NON-multisampled reference the same shader reaches 92.4% within 1/255 over 13,069 pooled agent-interior pixels (mean 0.88/255), which localises most of the remaining gap in MSAA sample positions -- GPU-specific, not recoverable by fitting -- rather than in shading. Three mechanisms were tried and are recorded so they are not retried: the fixed-function composition (FIXED - specular is additive and white and the texture modulates the whole primary colour, which took wall tops from 13/255 worst to 2/255 and made vertical wall faces bit-exact); Gouraud interpolation over MuJoCo's sphere/capsule tessellation (REFUTED - ten (slices, stacks, phase, diagonal) variants all scored 0.0-0.2% exact against 1.6% for plain per-pixel, which is also what sub-pixel triangles predict); and a mis-shaped specular lobe (REFUTED - a 24-knot piecewise-linear lobe fitted under four light/specular geometries, headlight directional or point crossed with Blinn or Phong, could not explain floor and agent with one curve).

Piecewise.name: swm-piecewise
Piecewise.parity_note: 1 ulp of exp, not geometry. Run on the CPU with the reference's own float32 exp this renderer reproduces the official frame BIT FOR BIT and the device contributes nothing (measured both ways); the residual is entirely that our exp is correctly rounded and torch's CPU float32 exp is only faithful. That ulp changes a pixel only where the dot's colour equals the background, because 255*(1-a)+255*a is the identity in exact arithmetic and not in float32, and the 41 px Gaussian tail is flat enough that the reference's own 3x3 neighbourhood cannot see the quantisation contour. Worst of 800 seeded draws: 2 pixels of 2.3 million, 1/255, one channel. See the module docstring.
Piecewise.doc:
``swm/Piecewise-v0`` at its shipped appearance: one open room, four invisible bias zones.

The zones are the whole point of the env and they are invisible by default — ``render_zones``
ships as 0 — so the frame is background, a 4 px border and the agent dot. That is a *feature* for
a world model (the dynamics are not readable off the pixels) and it is why the tinted
configuration is registered separately as ``PiecewiseZones`` rather than folded in here.

TwoRoom.parity_note: 1 ulp of exp, not geometry. Run on the CPU with the reference's own float32 exp this renderer reproduces the official frame BIT FOR BIT and the device contributes nothing (measured both ways); the residual is entirely that our exp is correctly rounded and torch's CPU float32 exp is only faithful. That ulp changes a pixel only where the dot's colour equals the background, because 255*(1-a)+255*a is the identity in exact arithmetic and not in float32, and the 41 px Gaussian tail is flat enough that the reference's own 3x3 neighbourhood cannot see the quantisation contour. Worst of 800 seeded draws: 2 pixels of 2.3 million, 1/255, one channel. See the module docstring.

``swm/TwoRoom-v1`` at its shipped appearance: two rooms, a wall with doors, no target drawn.

official env produces it as ``_render_frame(agent_pos=target_position)``, i.e. this same renderer
at a different state — so a corpus of agent positions regenerates the goals too.

DMCWalkerWalk.name: dmc-walker-walk

visual_fidelity.measured_at: 84 px, 64 states per domain from sample_states (the domain's own initialize_episode plus a 0-40 step random-action rollout), default appearance, H200 / driver 590.48.01 / MUJOCO_GL=egl, mujoco 3.11.0 + mujoco-warp 3.11.0, against dm_control's physics.render at camera 0

DMCWalkerWalk.visual_note: The frame is MJWarp's raytrace of the same scene, not dm_control's own raster. Two named mechanisms carry the residual, both measured per surface off MuJoCo's segmentation buffer: (1) the skybox is an 800x4800 gradient with mark="random" specks and MJWarp samples it with one unfiltered tap, which is 48-89% of the frame on cheetah/hopper/walker at mean 4.1-4.7/255 and is what holds SSIM down; (2) the checker floor is MINIFIED and MJWarp has no level-of-detail selection, so where MuJoCo's mipmap shows one grey (far-band luminance spread 0.1 on humanoid) MJWarp paints full contrast (9.7). Suitable for generating training data live -- the frame is a function of the state and the appearance knobs are per-environment tensors. NOT a substitute for a stored dataset when a policy will be evaluated on official dm_control pixels: the train and eval pixel distributions differ by the amount above and nothing here measures what that costs a policy. Closing it needs plane-texture level-of-detail in mujoco_warp's render kernel, which needs ray differentials it does not compute.
